activity_label.en: Preparation of the European Council meeting of 15-16 October 2026 (debate)
Effective measures to protect and empower children in the digital world (debate)

api:xmlFragment.en:
Laura Ballarín Cereza (S&D).

Madam President, when you ask a child today who he talks to when he is sad, one in two will tell you with a chatbot, with a machine. And it's not hard to understand why.

For many children, artificial intelligence is becoming the perfect confidant, always available, never judges and always gives you the reason. But here's the problem, what looks like companionship becomes slavery, because that listening comes at a price: emotional dependence, isolation and a mind that gets used to not thinking for itself. Our children cannot grow up learning that a machine is their best confidant.

Faced with this reality, we welcome the EU KIDS ACT that obliges chatbots and artificial intelligence colleagues to guarantee the highest levels of security and privacy for children under eighteen and also a digital minimum age, and prohibits addictive designs for minors. We have to regulate at European level and this goes beyond AI, also social networks and also video games, because we cannot ask our children to learn to set limits while the technologies themselves are designed not to have them.

So we need an emergency brake for our children, but also a Digital Fairness Act that combats addictive designs for adults. We are asked to do so by our families and also by an entire generation.

activity_label.en: Effective measures to protect and empower children in the digital world (debate)

api:xmlFragment.en:
Dóra Dávid (PPE).

Dear Madam President, We now see that excessive social media use can not only cause addiction and anxiety, but also affect children’s academic performance based on devastating PISA results. So now we really have to take action. The Internet has many advantages, but it is not designed for children. The goal is to make the online space safe and teach children how to use it responsibly. A comprehensive toolbox is needed to address this issue: education, awareness-raising, effective implementation of existing legislation and remedying legal gaps. For this latter, the EU Kids Act will be an important instrument.

I am pleased that the Commission reflects Parliament's position in many places, for example on a single European social media age, the suppression of feeds based on profiling, safe planning and the inclusion of AI chatbots and video games. But let’s not forget about gambling-like elements in video games, such as loot boxes, which are not covered by the Commission’s current draft. If children are not allowed to enter the casino in the real world, then why would we let them in there in the online space? The Kids Act draft is a good basis for making the online space safe for children and helping them navigate it with confidence.

activity_label.en: Effective measures to protect and empower children in the digital world (debate)

api:xmlFragment.en:
Nikolina Brnjac (PPE).

The Honourable Chair therefore does not know if we are all aware, but according to Unicef data, 1.2 million children reported sexual abuse in 2025 alone. deepfake content.

That is why their protection cannot be the sole responsibility of the parents. Digital platforms must also take responsibility.

We need security by design, effective good age protection and strong enforcement of the new rules proposed by the European Commission with the Child Act, which I strongly support. In particular, we need to respond to addictive design, harmful content, cyberbullying and the new risks posed by AI.

At the same time, we need to invest in the digital literacy of children, parents, but also teachers. Our goal must not be to distance children from technology, but to ensure that technology works for them, not against them.

activity_label.en: Effective measures to protect and empower children in the digital world (debate)

api:xmlFragment.en:
Henna Virkkunen, Executive Vice-President of the Commission.

Madam President, honourable Members, thank you very much for your interventions. It was very good to listen to the different views expressed today here. I think that today's debate has shown the determination of this House to make the online world a safer place for everybody, but especially for children and the generations to come.

Many of you underlined how important a part of our everyday life the digital world is nowadays, and I very much agree on that. So it is also important to remember all the time – and this is part of our Kids Act – that children also have the right to be connected with friends. They also have the right to have access to information. And that is why we haven't proposed anything like a blanket ban on digital services. But we have proposed here gradual access to really ensure that the content that the kids have access to is age‑appropriate.

We are also prohibiting harmful practices, and here we are speaking, for example, about very excessive screen time, which is very much connected to the addictive design of the services. We are also looking at the kind of content that is recommended for children and also who can see their content, who can be in contact with them. We have to look at these kinds of harmful functionalities and features when we speak about safety by design.

Global and European attention has very much been focused on the age limits. It's an important part of our proposal, and I think it is also very important that we are also able to show that we have an age verification tool also, that you can verify your age without giving your personal data for online platforms. We know that not everyone has had this. So those who have been imposing age limits in other countries outside Europe, they haven't had an age verification tool. It has been a big loophole, but we have one.

I would like to underline that a very important part of our Kids Act is exactly what many of you were calling for: safety by design – all digital services that minors are using, they have to be safe by design. And this is going further, not only covering social media platforms, but also video games and AI chatbots and companions. We have a tailor‑made list for those services laying down the dos and don'ts – what kind of practices there shouldn't be and what there should be – to be included in these features to make sure that they are safe by design.

A very big part of this proposal is really that now we are turning this around, that the social media platforms really have to show beforehand that they are complying with our rules, because now we have a very clear and precise list of the practices which should and shouldn't take place when minors are using those services.

Some of you asked why it's taking so much time to enforce the DSA. When we speak about the DSA, it's horizontal legislation covering all digital services. We have to respect the legal procedure when we are enforcing the rules. So we have to gather evidence, we have to gather information, we also have to have a strong legal basis, and we also have to respect due process. And it's taking time. But now we have very precise rules when it comes to protection of minors and we are complementing our DSA. We continue, of course, to enforce the DSA all the time, but when it comes to the protection of minors, we have very precise rules. They have to come beforehand and show with the compliance plan how they are changing the design of their service.

We are also launching here this fast process for enforcement only in 90 days, because we have also a clear list now that we can check to see if the practices are in place or not. Thank you very much to everybody for the very good contributions to this discussion.

András László (PfE).

Dear Madam President, It is absurd that part of the European Parliament expects China to solve Europe's problems. Let's look at the facts. China's GDP is almost equal to that of the EU. The scissors have been steadily closed for the past 15 years. China has cheaper electricity, more industrial robots, more new AI investments and patents. And what hurts Europe the most today: The share of Chinese cars in the world market is growing rapidly. And bilateral trade shows a deficit of one billion euros per day at the expense of Europe.

Looking ahead, you can hardly expect a trend reversal. China's economy will overtake the European Union. Let's not fool ourselves, let's not look for a scapegoat. The economic weakness of the EU is not caused by China, but is due to EU rules. Only Europe will stand up for Europe's interests.

But the only way to defend our political and commercial interests is to put the European economy in order first. We need to reduce anti-industrial green rules and administrative burdens that stifle businesses. Only in this way can Europe remain a meaningful player in the world.

(The speaker is willing to answer several blue card questions)

activity_label.en: EU strategies for islands, coastal communities and outermost regions (debate)

api:xmlFragment.en:
Valérie Deloge (PfE).

Madam President, you like to come there for your holidays, you stay for fifteen days, you enjoy the landscapes, the climate. Then you leave as if nothing had happened. But for the 17 million Europeans who live there all year round, the reality is very different. They do not want to be the forgotten of Europe. Water, transport, agriculture, climate, dock dues, all these issues take on a very different dimension in our ORs. What we sometimes consider simple on the mainland can become a real challenge on an island.

The Commission itself recognises the cost of insularity with transport being up to 300% more expensive. Budgets exist, but that is not enough to compensate for these constraints. The needs are very concrete. Access to water and sanitation infrastructure remain major issues. Sargassum strandings and their consequences hit the West Indies hard.

For the post-2027 period, we refuse to allow support for our territories to be drowned in major global plans. In agriculture, POSEI must remain an investment in its own right. The EAFRD should continue to finance farm investment and modernisation. We are in 2026 at the time of AI, and our ORs are still the neglected of Europe.
